items.author: Angela Alagna
items.bodyText: 7hShame on each and every one of you! Our children love their school mostly because of their teachers. This video was created before the school year started while most of these AMAZING people were there prepping for the upcoming school year. And it hyped our kids up. They were excited to go to school and that’s not easy at this age. Find something better to do with your time than complain about some of the hardest working and most caring people in our community. Who are just trying to get everyone ready and excited for the year.LikeReply

items.author: Joy Hankey
items.bodyText: 12hJennifer Brinker there is a place and time for "fun". And it should be appropriate for the role you are in in a child's life. Boundaries are needed in certain situations.LikeReply

items.author: Jennifer Brinker
items.bodyText: 11hI think being fun like this is appropriate for children. I would not find it as appropriate for say… a financial advisor. Fascinating that you see otherwise.LikeReply

items.author: Nicole Ashraf
items.bodyText: 21hJane Puszkar that’s an interesting comment. Test scores in my building and grade level have gone up astronomically in the past few years. Also, please remember that kids are far more than a test score. That goes for teachers too. Their ability to teach and reach children can be evaluated by much more than a standardized test score.LikeReply

items.author: Nicole Ashraf
items.bodyText: 49mJoy Hankey I can assure you that the standard of the test has not been lowered. In fact, in my 14 years of teaching, I have watched state assessments become increasingly rigorous and require students to demonstrate much deeper levels of thinking.And yes, our job is to teach children, but teaching and reaching children are not mutually exclusive. Students cannot effectively learn when they do not feel safe, supported, and connected at school. Maslow’s hierarchy of needs has long demonstrated that basic needs such as safety and belonging must be met before students are able to fully engage in learning.What has changed in recent years is that the district is finally providing teachers with resources that are much more closely aligned with Missouri state standards and evidence-based literacy practices, including the Science of Reading. When teachers have strong, standards-aligned curriculum and students feel safe enough to learn, that is when meaningful academic growth happens.Now that we have a decent reading resource, I’m hopeful that we can get an aligned math resource. We haven’t had math resources aligned with our state standards since 2011 (at least in elementary). Reaching children is part of teaching them.LikeReplyEdited
